assertions.interpretation: The scene is set at the time when Tao Kan (陶公) was gravely ill, near death.
At the time of his grave illness, Tao Kan offered no words of remonstrance or advice to the court, which the court officials resented.
The court officials at that time regarded Tao Kan's silence as a grievance.
Ren Zu (仁祖, i.e., Xie Shang) heard about this matter and commented on it, a moment subsequent to the court officials' grievance.
Ren Zu's remark refers to the current time (the time of Tao Kan's illness) as having no Shu Diao, i.e., no treacherous eunuch figure.
The worthies of the time subsequently regarded Ren Zu's words as virtuous speech, a later evaluation of his remark.
In his final memorial, Tao Kan states he was nearly eighty years old and had reached the highest ministerial rank—a self-description at the time of his death.

assertions.exact_span: 猶冀犬馬之齒尚可少延
assertions.interpretation: In his final memorial, Tao Kan still hoped his life might be extended a little longer—expressing his state of mind at the time of writing.

assertions.interpretation: The Lüshi Chunqiu anecdote about Guan Zhong and Shu Diao records that Shu Diao later indeed threw Qi into disorder—a later outcome cited as precedent.

assertion.exact_span: 侃少有遠槩綱維宇宙之志
assertion.interpretation: Background: In his youth, Tao Kan already had far-reaching aspirations to order the cosmos.

assertion.interpretation: Background: Tao Kan successively rose to become governor of the three provinces of Xiang, Guang, and Jing.
Tao Kan's memorial recalls that he had received extraordinary favors from the former reigns across successive generations—background preceding his final illness.
